records.title: Show HN: DBDelve – Open-Source DB Client Made with Rust and GPUI
records.author: shayan_abbas
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m Shayan and a few months ago I started building a DB Client DBDelve with a focus on performance and just making something that feels good to use (in the spirit of Zed, Ghostty, and other tools that just feel pleasant to use).

For my workflow I’ve always looked for performance, especially since some time ago I had a really outdated machine and any kind of bloat was really noticeable, I remember using DBeaver and it just crashing on me multiple times, I also had to use postGIS which just made it worse. I migrated all my essential dev tools to use the ones with performance in mind (Zed, Ghostty etc) but the only thing that was missing was DB Client. The main choices everyone has are DBeaver which is a memory hog and an overkill for most of the tasks imo. The other options like Datagrid, Beekeeper, TablePlus are either electron based so bloated and memory hogs or paid and closed-source.

DBDelve 0.3.6 against DBeaver 25.3.1 on the same Postgres table, median of 5 runs each (2026-10-11, M1 Pro, 32 GB). Times are from the action to the rows rendered.

                            DBDelve   DBeaver
  Launch                    1.1 s     5.2 s
  Idle memory               133 MB    606 MB
  1,000-row query           0.21 s    1.96 s
  1M rows, time             56 s      208 s
  1M rows, memory [1]       4.9 GB    17 GB
[1] The whole 1M-row, 100-column table pulled into memory on purpose, with the row limit off. Not a normal use case; DBeaver's heap limit had to be raised manually for the benchmark.

Scrolling perf with 1 million rows loaded with 100 columns each: https://youtu.be/V2MOhJYFqIE

It has most of the features most devs would need for 90% of their workflow plus some more I thought would be a nice touch: Readonly, read-write and Full Access modes Glass themes (If you’re into them, I am) Keyboard focused with every keybinding customizable Organization of connections into projects

Me and some other folks have been daily driving it for more than a month now and most good feedback comes on it having a really simple UI to navigate, very stable for its age and the performance of course. I’m also sharing here because those people tell me this has potential to grow so I’m trying my hand at distributing it.

Just want to give a huge shoutout here to the Zed team for GPUI, it's a breeze to work with if you just get through them not updating the crate officially on crates.io but the community has found the solutions for it, you just have to dig deep for it. It performs extremely well and just the HTML-like structure of it, makes it easy to understand for someone from a web dev background and agents are very good at writing it too. GPUI component also solves a lot of problems with having a good component library we can use. I think for anyone starting a GPUI project now, GPUI-kit makes a lot of sense, it just bundles GPUI, GPUI-component together and has some optimizations adding retained mode which is experimental but could provide a lot of benefit, so think all things considered it should be the default way.

The major optimization I did was just lowering the memory overhead by using packed rows which reduced the memory usage by 40% on large datasets (8.1GB to 4.9GB on a 4GB table loaded in app), everything else came bundled in with Rust and GPUI mostly or they just made it very easy.

Limitations: It's not signed and notarized, identity verification from apple's side has been a nightmare but it should be signed soon. Don’t expect feature parity with more mature clients for now, the general direction of this right now is the zed way of adding features in but after making sure the core workflows are done with a high quality.

Do give it a try, you can import your connections from dbeaver and tableplus.

https://github.com/ShayanAbbas1/dbdelve

records.title: Show HN: Vork – headless 3D and VFX engine for agents
records.author: raviparikh
records.storyText:
I made an agent-native 3d/vfx engine.

Agents are good at making interesting scenes in Blender/Unreal/Nuke/etc. But these tools are fundamentally limited compared to what coding agents are capable of. Many simplifying assumptions are baked into these tools in order to fit human authoring methods.

In vork, agents write the whole scene as code, including their own shaders, materials, cameras and physics, and vork renders it on the GPU. The core API fits in about 2,500 tokens.

So, for example, almost every 3d engine assumes light moves in a straight line. Light near a black hole does not; so the best you can do in e.g. Blender is faking gravitational lensing. In vork, you can model it for real.

If you want a camera lens that simulates a dragonfly's eye, or realistically-modeled Fata Morgana, this is also possible in vork.

records.title: Show HN: Totle, daily math puzzle game; Saturday puzzles have the fewest answers
records.author: zemelett
records.storyText:
My oldest two kids are off to college and since leaving we've been playing the Wordle and 'sharing' our solutions with each other. It's been a fun way to stay connected with them, and it's become a bit of a challenge to see if we can beat each other's solutions. This got me thinking about other ways I could connect with them. The thing about the Wordle is that it doesn't take a large commitment of time, you can just pull it out when you've a few spare minutes. So I set out to build a game that would borrow from many of the themes that keep pulling us back to Wordle. What I created is called Tōtle which fits another one of our (okay my) favorite things; Dad jokes and puns (as it’s pronounced total).

Here's how it works. You get five different numbers from a number pool 1 to 20, and a target from the remaining pool. Combine two at a time with + − × ÷, using all five numbers, every result a positive whole number, each puzzle always takes 4 moves. You get 3 rounds and 4 undos per round; a medal for fewest moves (perfect 4 = crown). There's a spoiler-free share card, like Wordle’s grid.

The combinatorics math works out like this: C(20,5) (that's choose 5 from 20) × 15 possible target numbers = 232,560 possible puzzles. An interesting side quest: exhaustive search discovered that exactly 6 can’t be solved. They all are from the group of 6 numbers: 3, 7, 16, 17, 19, 20. If any one of those is chosen as the target the other 5 cannot make the target. I'm not sure if there are any interesting reasons or patterns.

Every puzzle was sorted into 7 difficulty bands, by how many solutions each has, to provide a way to add increasing difficulty along the week. Sunday draws from the easiest 30%, Saturday from the hardest 3%, the game shows “harder than X% of puzzles” on the hardest days; Saturdays so far have been in the 98th–99th percentile of difficulty. 5 Saturdays were discovered to have exactly one answer (answer here means ways that only regroup or reorder the same moves count as one); the first is #68, Saturday, December 19, 2026.

A few things I'd love to know from y'all:

Difficulty: does the Sunday-to-Saturday curve feel right, and are Saturdays too hard? I've experimented with a mode that offers some help. But it's still under development.

First-time play: was anything confusing, like dragging vs. tapping or how rounds work?

Phones: How does it play on your phone vs your computer?

records.title: Show HN: Brick Atlas: Explore 1000+ LEGO sets on one zoomable canvas
records.author: gasi
records.storyText:
Hello HN, I’m Daniel and I run ZoomHub, a small deep zoom image service.

Most online catalogs look the same: There’s a grid of thumbnails, limited to about 20–50 items, filters that refresh the page when activated, and pagination buttons to go to page 22 of 128. It has always bothered me that you can’t see the whole collection and every action makes you wait and lose context.

I built Brick Atlas to show it doesn’t have to be that way: You can browse 1000+ LEGO sets by zooming in, selecting a set, seeing different angles (at full resolution) and in the sidebar, the set’s piece count, price, etc. You can read the whole instructions (on some sets) without ever seeing a page refresh or losing your place. On a slow connection, the image simply gradually becomes sharper. Once you are done, you can zoom out and see all sets again. Apply a price filter to find gift ideas under $50 or switch to Real size layout to see how big the sets are in real life compared to each other. Toggle Box vs Built to switch between the retail box and the assembled set. For collectors, I added the scatter view to plot sets by piece count vs price so you can find the best value sets. Every change in filters or layout animates gently so you never lose the thread.

I’ve been obsessed with zooming for almost twenty years. I interned at Zoomorama and later worked on the (Microsoft Live Labs) Seadragon team, in case this looks familiar to you :)

The idea to use zoom and image streaming could be applied to photo galleries, a museum catalog, other products, or even scientific images. I just happened to pick LEGO because I’m an AFOL (adult fan of LEGO), have been wanting to explore their catalog like this for years, and hope there are lots of you who do too.

I published this as a static data set to S3 behind CloudFront (700k WebP tiles) for performance and render it using OpenZoom, my own WebGL deep zoom engine. The data comes from Brickset (thanks to Huw, the founder, for his blessing) and the images from LEGO (also via Brickset). I used my ‘free’ Anthropic API credits from Ultra plan to classify images into box vs built, to extract tags and colors, etc. using Claude Haiku and Sonnet (spend: ~$60.)

I’d love to hear how it feels to explore, what you’d do differently, and what collection you’d like to see this used with :)

records.title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
records.author: apiclay
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy.

Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist.

ApiClay makes that whole loop easier.

You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live.

But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace.

If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links.

You can also turn what you already have into an API:

* MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints.

* Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API.

* Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing.

* Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products.

For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data.

There are also practical data tools beyond discovery:

* Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result.

* Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes.

* Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs.

* Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper.

For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use.

*ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.*

We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

records.title: Show HN: You can now train your own LLMs with less memory, on your consumer GPUs
records.author: gladia-solaria
records.storyText:
*TL;DR: You can train your own 27B model on a 3090 with 24GB VRAM, though you would have to go through hundreds of billions of tokens for it to be good. I am working on conversion of existing models. Check repos for code and the paper if you are interested in more. I have a 40.4GB Qwen Flash* N*ext GGUF*

Hi, I do AI research. I have been working on an optimizer that doesn't need the \~16 bytes of VRAM per weight to train a model that AdamW does. I focused on training ternary networks bcs BitNet (Ma et al.) shows they match full precision quality in large scales. The problem is BitNet also keeps the full precision weights during training which means you still need to use the same amount of memory. I got this down from 16 bytes to 1 byte or even less per weight.

For you, this means, you can train your own 10-20B parameter models on your consumer GPUs. I fitted 27B model training on a single 24GB 3090 and a 23B model on a 16GB GPU. The trained model costs \~1.6 bits per weight (\~6GB at 27B), 10x smaller than 16bit, and 5x smaller than Q8.

I have also been working on converting existing models and training them. This is harder and I am still working on it but I have some promising results. I quantized and trained a Qwen3.8 27B though the file I published below has adapters which are about 2GBs, pushing the file size to 8GB. I am also making a no-adapter version right now. It scores GSM8K 0.895, the same as full precision, HumanEval 0.84 vs 0.93 and runs on a 12 GB GPU at \~2*3* tok/s on my crippled 12GB laptop 4080, though this number can heavily be improved with custom kernels, engineering, etc. I will leave it to you guys to help me with that too.

I also quantized and trained Qwen Flash Next down to 40.4 GBs including its n-gram table (at 8GB). It largely retains the skills of the network (scores equivalent on GSM8K benchmark, a little behind on HumanEval, I unfortunately don't have compute for the larger benchmarks such as TerminalBench2.1 but perhaps some of you can help me out) but forgets facts. It mostly works fine if you give it web search as far as my experience goes but this is not strictly measured.

I am still doing work on this and I will keep working on it, perhaps even for many years. The code is open for non-commercial use. Check out:

The core repo for training: https://github.com/oguzeldereli/ttf-ternary

The repo for conversion: https://github.com/oguzeldereli/ttf-conversion

Repo for running models trained by ttf: https://github.com/oguzeldereli/ttf-home

GGUF for a converted Qwen 3.8 27B with adapters (around 8 GB): https://huggingface.co/oguzeldereli/ttf-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF

GGUF for a converted Qwen 3.8 Flash Next (around 40.4GB): https://huggingface.co/oguzeldereli/ttf-Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-G...

GGUF for a converted Qwen 3.8 27B without adapters (around 6 GB): Currently in conversion and will drop soon.

I will convert a Qwen 4 27B instance when it drops.

Full paper: https://github.com/oguzeldereli/ttf-ternary/blob/main/paper/...

Also, I would appreciate github stars if you like the project.

records.title: Show HN: QueenMQ – slow LLM calls blocked our Kafka partitions, so we built it
records.author: aliceviola
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Alice.

Over the last year, at Smartness, the company where I work, we built a new message broker, open source under Apache 2.0. During this year it has replaced Kafka almost completely for us. I would like to show it to you and try to explain what is different about it.

First, long story short: in 2025 we launched a new product in our suite. Like all the others it used Kafka for messaging, and like many other companies we were using Kafka as a message queue, wrongly and knowingly.

In this product head-of-line blocking hurt a lot: an LLM call takes seconds to minutes, and it blocked every other chat in the same partition. We first built a hack: we saved the Kafka messages in Postgres, ordered by the entity we needed (a chat_id, for example), processed them, and sent them back to Kafka. Then we decided to build a real broker on that idea. It took a year, from C++ plus Postgres to, today, a single Rust binary with data replicated on disk by Raft.

I designed this system, so I am biased. Still, I believe QueenMQ holds a new paradigm that turns a message broker into something more powerful, while staying simple.

What QueenMQ is, compared to what you already know:

Like Kafka, it has partitions, but in QueenMQ they are dynamic (not preallocated) and you can use a lot of them (tested up to 10 million). Like Kafka it is a log, but there is one Raft leader per tenant, so all of a tenant's writes go through one node, which allows transactions without 2PC. Head-of-line blocking can only happen inside one partition, which is one business entity, like a customer or a chat. If you need a plain queue, you can use a different partition for every message.

Like RabbitMQ, it has ACK, NACK, retries and a DLQ: this makes it a message queue. It has no routing on push and no exchanges, though.

Like a database: thanks to its etcd-like design, it runs transactions that include ACKs, pushes to other queues, KV writes and timers, and it has atomic locks. The KV store is replicated by Raft and keeps the application's state. It is linearizable.

It also has strong streaming features: the SDKs can receive one single log with all the messages of all the queues, with one clock and one order. On top of it there are the classic streaming features, like windows, and some less common ones.

Clients talk to it over HTTP (the clients are thin, the intelligence is in the broker), and it is Kafka-compatible (although that way you cannot use all of its strengths).

The idea underneath is the change from seeing a message broker as a pure "handler" of messages to one where you can offload a lot of application logic that you would otherwise write yourself. In our company it let us remove outbox tables, cron jobs and many other things.

On three beefy machines (24 vCPU, NVMe, 88 GB of RAM), QueenMQ sustains 3M msg/s of 256-byte messages, up to 10M partitions, with p99 latency around 20 ms and every write fsynced on two nodes. Of course, with a single leader per tenant, it does not scale by adding more machines.

We tested it hard: 226 tests of our own, written with the Jepsen library, on up to 5 nodes.

It is changing the way we design the systems and products of our company.

I believe in this project and I believe in open source, and I am really glad that Smartness thinks the same way. It is hard to find the time and the money to build something like this without a company behind you.

I would love to get questions, the harsh ones too (like how many times this thing crashed production), and feedback.

records.author: abelw
records.storyText:
After installing the web extension and clicking its icon it shows a QR code that is scanned by a phone which opens the web app in the browser. When the WebRTC connection has been set up between the devices you can steer a dot on the computer web page by holding a button and pointing the phone. The app also has other presentation clicker features like switching slides, drawing, presenter notes, and can also be used for remote controlling some videos (tested on YouTube and Plex).

Firefox extension: https://addons.mozilla.org/sv-SE/firefox/addon/clikr/

Chrome extension: https://chromewebstore.google.com/detail/clikr/oalndbmcbpchb...

Home page: https://www.clikr.app/

I've always been fascinated in how much the web can do. This project started as a fun small POC many years ago when some of these native app-like functions were less common. I got the idea to see if I could make my phone control a "laser dot" on my computer just by tilting the phone like a real laser pointer. Being a web guy I went with web extension + web app. Surprisingly I think I got the basics working in an afternoon or two, having some experience with web extensions from before. Getting the user experience smooth and stable and adding other presentation features in various online tools took more time...

It uses RTCPeerConnection for the communication, Metered for TURN, and a small protocol for the commands (point, switch slides, etc.). The deviceorientation event is used for getting the orientation (which has to be explicitly allowed on some devices). One issue here is that the angle values don't actually mean anything without a reference. Therefore the first pair of angles received in the extension becomes the origin for that "pointing". The origin on the screen is the middle of the viewport and additional received angles move the dot with those origin values as reference. I.e. it will always start in the middle. This is of course not as good as a real laser pointer but I think it works quite well when you've tried it a bit. Distance to the screen and its size will matter for how much to move the dot which is why there is also a calibration tool.

I like the other features too but I think the laser pointer is the fun one.

There are some paid features (one-time payment, no subscription) but the laser pointer, basic presentation features, and video remote are free and doesn't require an account.

It has some users but it's hard to get them to give feedback so honestly I don't yet know much about how it's performing in real situations. If anyone here tries it out please tell me what you think.

Valin was born - an application that allows users to share to it (almost) any kind of contents from applications (videos, audio, links, papers, reels. etc) and it goes in and using on-device AI transcribes audio, extract key frames of the video, extracts text from the frames and shows Key Takeaways and Summary. - supports videos, audio, pdf, images

- Embeddings Gemma 300m - for clustering, collection generation and semantic search

          ["actionType","your search term",""],

          ["actionSleep", "2", ""]

      "cache": "1d",
      "format": "json",
      "extraction": {
          "results": {
          "$xpath": "//div[contains(@class, 'MjjYud')]",

records.title: Show HN: Negs (Spektrafilm) brings spectral film simulations to the browser
records.author: haasisnoah
records.storyText:
Hi HN, I'm Noah. Negs runs spektrafilm, Andrea Volpato's physically based film simulation, in your browser (it's completely rewritten in Rust and using WebGPU). Drop in a photo (JPEG, PNG, TIFF or a RAW), pick a film and a print paper, and drag the sliders. The picture updates as you drag, and nothing is uploaded: it all runs on your machine.

Try it: https://getnegs.com/try/

Code (GPLv3): https://github.com/noahhaasis/negs

There are also native apps on the same engine: SwiftUI on macOS, GTK4 on Linux, and Windows.

Spektrafilm (it started life as agx-emulsion) isn't a LUT or a preset. It simulates the whole analog chain, negative and then print, using only the manufacturers' published datasheets. Andrea's original write-up on discuss.pixls.us is worth reading in full: https://discuss.pixls.us/t/spectral-film-simulations-from-sc.... Roughly, it goes like this:

- Your RGB image is turned back into a light spectrum and exposed onto the film's three dye layers through their published spectral sensitivity curves. - Each layer builds up density along its characteristic curve. Datasheet curves are measured with densitometers that see all three dyes at once, so they're first separated into a curve for each layer. - DIR couplers: where one layer develops a lot of density, it releases inhibitors that hold back development nearby, in the same layer and the ones next to it. This is where film's saturation and its edge sharpness come from. - Grain is simulated per layer, with fast and slow sub-layers, as random silver halide particles that become dye clouds. It depends on the density at each spot instead of being laid over the image. - Halation: light passes through the emulsion, bounces off the film base and exposes the red layer again (it's at the back), which gives the red glow around highlights. - The negative's dye spectra are then projected through a virtual enlarger with Y/M filtration onto print paper, which has its own sensitivities and curves, and the print is scanned back to RGB.

Because it's a model, the controls are physical: camera exposure, print exposure, enlarger filters, how much DIR coupling, grain particle size, halation strength. Push them too far and the image breaks the way film does, with colour crossovers when it's badly over- or underexposed. And you can experimentw with each control. There are about 50 stocks: Portra, Ektar, Gold, Pro 400H, Superia, Kodachrome, Velvia and Provia slide film, Aerochrome and some B&W (HP5, FP4...). There are 9 papers and print films too, such as Endura, Crystal Archive and Vision 2383. The paper choice has a huge impact on the final look.

Negs implements the entire chain and is orders of magnitudes faster than the original python Spektrafilm implementation, so you can play around with sliders and get live feedback.

Feedback is very welcome, especially from people who have actually shot these stocks: tell me which ones look wrong to you.

records.title: Show HN: Git-dupe – plain Git per-project private versioning for agent files
records.author: WayHow
records.storyText:
Hi HN!

Suppose you have notes, skills, and agent instructions that are part of your personal workflow, so you do not want them committed to the public repo, but at the same time, you want them to be in the workspace at the correct locations (e.g., AGENTS.md file locations matter), and these files cannot be simply gitignored because you also want versioning for them.

The solution to this is actually just a bit more plain Git.

  $ git status --short                                 # public repo
  ?? AGENTS.md
  ?? notes/

  $ git dupe init                                      # private repo
  Initialized empty Git repository in /home/brian/code/project/.git/dupe/

  $ git dupe add notes/ AGENTS.md                      # private repo
  hint: notes is now hidden from the project's Git; run from the root, 'git dupe unhide -- notes' stops hiding it

  $ git dupe commit -m "Notes and agent instructions"  # private repo
  [main (root-commit) 3eb3af9] Notes and agent instructions
   3 files changed, 3 insertions(+)
   create mode 100644 .gitdupe
   create mode 100644 AGENTS.md
   create mode 100644 notes/todo.md

  $ git status --short                                 # public repo: nothing

  $ git dupe log --oneline                             # private repo: your files
  3eb3af9 Notes and agent instructions
The solution, in short, is versioning those agent files in a repo, say <private-repo> (this repo is private to you and holds the history for your agent files), and that repo shares the same worktree as the public repo <public-repo>. You essentially overlap the two, with <private-repo> put in .git/ (and .git/ is that of the public repo) for a convenient solution.

If you want to read more about the strategy used, there is more comprehensive documentation in the repo.

git-dupe supports macOS, Linux, and Windows and is under the MIT License.

records.title: Show HN: A media server designed to be hosted on a VPS [more in the text]
records.author: maury91
records.storyText:
I've been working on this project for the last 2 years, this is the second iteration and this iteration was designed with the intent of being deployed into a VPS.

Let's walk backwards from the worst case to the realistic case.

1a. The absolute worst case, someone takes a memory dump of your VPS, well you are screwed if something fishy is going on they will find about it.

1b. Someone mounts the .qcow2 image and inspects your VPS like if its a docker image without leaving any trace, also in this case, you are screwed.

So we can already say, this project is not to defend you once you become a target, that's already too late.

Now let's see what can be actually done.

Someone takes a file system dump, yes we can work with this.

An automated script looks around the file system for something fishy, yes this is literally the use case.

But how to achieve this?

First we need to decide what an actor wants to detect in our media server:

- media files: if you do not have authorization to host them, this is the absolute worst. So how to tackle this?

First step: The project encrypts them, each media file is always persisted encrypted, the encryption key is a combination of a general encryption key, and a random value stored in the database. If you have both of them you can decrypt the file, if even only one is missing they cannot be decrypted.

At this point it becomes important what level of safety we want...

Do you want to stop automated scripts? The database can live in the VPS, unless a script is targeting exactly this project they will not be able to know that file X needs to be decrypted with Y

Do you want to be "safe" in case of a file system snapshot? The database then must be external to the VPS

Second step: The length of the media file is a giveaway, let's add some random padding to it.

- torrent info hashes, names, magnets, blobs, etc... This are in the gray zone, but a script could still treat the presence of a specific torrent infohash in your system as something to flag you for. We store them encrypted in the database, if you separate the database from the VPS then you have the decryption key in the VPS and the encrypted infohash in the database, a snapshot of the DB alone is not enough. Both VPS and DB are needed at the same time.

Yes, I'm aware this is not enough to stop a determined sysop, but this is not the purpose of it, the purpose is to never reach the point where they inspect you.

If this peculiarity of the project intrigues you, you can find out more about it at: https://github.com/maury91/miauflix

I do also have another feature I'm quite proud of, ahead-of-time downloads. I think the process of imdb_id -> torrent hash -> torrent file -> loading seeds -> download initial parts to be too long ( time wise ), so I worked for it to happen before you click "watch":

- catalog data ( TMDB/Trakt ) is constantly synched in backgrounds queues - sources are searched by priority in background queues - torrent health ( seeders/leachers ) are kept up-to-date periodically in background queues - torrent metadata is download in background queues and in case of mismatching data the torrent is deleted (a torrent containing movie_name.exe is marked as fake) - the initial sectors needed to stream a file are download when you enter the details page, if you don't click on "watch" like flash but you spend a little bit of time reading the description ( or in future watching the trailer ), everything will be warm and streaming can start immediately

I don't know if someone ever used it, but I contributed to webtorrent because when I was reloading a torrent it would make the server hang: https://github.com/webtorrent/webtorrent/pull/2878 [I was a little bit burn out at the time of this PR]

records.title: Show HN: VoxaDub – Open-source AI video dubbing with speaker-aware voices
records.author: kadirb4rut
records.storyText:
Hi HN,

I have been working on a project called VoxaDub: an open source local-first AI dubbing tool which can translate videos into other languages while preserving the original voices of the speakers.

A major issue when translating is ensuring the translation matches with the length of speech in the target language. Even slight differences in timing can cause unnatural dubbing. It becomes more complex when there are multiple speakers in the original video.

I have created a pipeline that uses Whisper/WhisperX to transcribe and align audio, Community-1 to identify speakers, Hy-MT2 to translate contextually and VoxCPM2 to generate speaker aware audio.

The main feature of VoxaDub is the ability to improve the translation using the available time for the audio to be spoken for, limit the time changes to within certain bounds and analyse for any timing issues.

There is also some experimental Live Dubbing for YouTube videos and live streams through a Chrome extension. This is actively being developed and is not yet production ready.

The main project runs fully locally once models are set up, no external translation or TTS APIs are required. Optional GPU usage is available using Colab and Modal.

I am pleased to see that the project was recently added to the Ecosystem & Community section of OpenBMB's official VoxCPM GitHub repository (PR #389). While this is just a community project listing it was nice to see this progress.

True examples of the English to Spanish, Japanese and Turkish dubbing can be found in the README. Source videos, information on how it was implemented and any limitations are also present.

The project is MIT licensed and can be found on GitHub.

I would really appreciate any technical feedback on the timing of the translations, speaker consistency and simplifying the local setup. There is a lot of room for improvement so any thoughts would be great!

records.storyText:
Inspired by Karpathy's HackerTube, I wondered what was buried in "What are you working on?" thread comments. I wanted to see what changed, and who was still at it years later. So, I built this site to answer some of those questions.

A couple of things you can do: type in your idea and see who already tried it, look up your username and see what you were working on in 2020, see who’s been working on the same thing for a decade, or what founders posted before they had a company.

I built it using Claude Code. Claude Sonnet read all 20,982 top-level replies and pulled out a name, description, topic and how AI was involved. One finding is that AI went from 1% of answers in 2009–11 to 33% this year.

A few limits of the result: labels are model output, and I only spot-checked them. The HN thread only went monthly in 2024, so early years are thin. If I’ve mislabeled your project, or you’d rather not be included, please tell me.

If you’ve been posting here for years, I’d love to hear what happened to those projects.

records.title: Show HN: Black Ops II statically recompiled to native ARM64 macOS
records.author: adrbn
records.storyText:
I recompiled the three Black Ops II executables (campaign, Zombies, multiplayer) from 32-bit x86 Windows to native ARM64 macOS, ahead of time. Remill lifts each function to LLVM IR, a set of custom passes rewrites it, and the result links against a hand-written Win32 runtime whose Direct3D 11 is drawn by Metal. No Wine, no Rosetta, no JIT, one process. About 150,000 functions are translated; anything the translation misses falls back to a small x86 interpreter, so a gap costs speed instead of crashing.

On an M1: campaign 51-60 fps, Zombies 57-60 on six maps, multiplayer against bots 53-60.

The repo contains no game files and no translated code. It converts your own Steam copy on your Mac, which takes about 1h45 on an M1.

Much of the work was done with AI coding agents, and I spent most of my time on verification: frame pacing against the game's own clock, byte checks on the input files, and run logs for every claim in the README.

It's a beta. Split-screen Zombies is the current work in progress. Happy to answer questions about the lifting, the Win32 runtime or the D3D11-to-Metal layer.
